# Abstract

This project compares Michael Jordan, Kobe Bryant and LeBron James using full
regular-season career statistics and U.S. television audiences for Finals series
featuring each player. The data contain three career summaries and 23 Finals
appearances. Jordan has the highest scoring average, while LeBron has the
highest rebound and assist averages. Jordan's Finals appearances have the
highest mean audience in these records. LeBron's mean audience exceeds Kobe's
when 2020 is excluded, demonstrating sensitivity to scope. Jersey-sales rankings
are supplementary.

# Introduction

How do these players compare in career production and the audiences for their
Finals appearances? We combine these ideas to see who performed best but as
well as who left a legacy that garnered fans to tune in on the game of 
basketball. We examine them as separate measurable dimensions instead of
assuming that one statistic defines greatness. The current analysis describes
the complete selected career snapshots and Finals records. It does not draw a
random sample of all possible basketball players or broadcasts.

# Executive summary

- Jordan leads career PPG; LeBron leads career RPG and APG among these players.
- Jordan's series-average Finals audience is the largest in the collected data.
- Removing 2020 changes the ordering of LeBron's and Kobe's audience means.
- Published jersey ranks lack the coverage and sales quantities needed for a
  career-wide three-player sales comparison.

# Data and methods

StatMuse supplies three full regular-season career summaries: games, points,
PPG, RPG, APG and shooting percentages. These are the retrieved
snapshot, not a live feed as Lebron is currently active on this list. Jordan's 
six seasonal performance rows were replaced
in the comparison by his career summary.

Sports Media Watch and Front Office Sports provide 23 Finals-series audience
records: Jordan (6), Kobe (7) and LeBron (10). Variables include player, year,
opponent, series games, championship result, audience, method and a pandemic
flag. Audience is average U.S. viewers per game in millions, not worldwide or
unique career viewers. Kobe and Jordan use reported series averages; LeBron
uses means of rounded game figures from the historical archive. This source
precision difference and historical measurement changes remain limitations.

The cleaning RMD trims names, converts numeric fields, checks duplicate keys
and missing required values, derives audience units and a 2020 flag, and saves
processed CSVs and an RData environment. It recomputes descriptive summaries.
The standardized input tables already reflect earlier collection and unit
conversion; this workflow does not recreate the original web extraction.
No valid Finals series was dropped. Unknown jersey quantities remain missing.

Six jersey-ranking entries and two Cleveland-return game audiences are retained
as supplementary records. The latter are excluded from Finals summaries.
Means and medians give each Finals series equal weight. A game-weighted mean
is also saved by the processing file; it is approximate for rounded source data.

# Further visualization and analysis plan

We plan on adding comparable Finals-specific player performance records if 
exploring performance versus audience; repeating career averages over Finals 
rows would not supply independent performance observations. As well as explore 
opponent, series length and television era before considering regression. This
can give context and maybe a sense of difficulty each player had to face, which
would add better support for the question of the better player.

# Limitations

Career lengths, playing roles, pace, teammates and rules differ. Finals-only
selection excludes seasons without an appearance. Television access and
measurement methods changed over time, and the pandemic shifted the 2020
schedule. Rounding and audience averaging methods differ across sources.
These conditions prevent causal attribution of audiences to a player and a
single definitive GOAT conclusion.
